name: Maitreyanātha

tradition.text: the bodhisattva Maitreya, regent of the Buddha, residing in the Tuṣita heaven

scholarly.text: if a human teacher, c. 4th c. CE; many scholars treat 'Maitreya' as a name under which Asaṅga's circle transmitted texts

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that the author is the bodhisattva Maitreya (tch:maitreya-bodhisattva), who appeared to Asaṅga after twelve years of fruitless meditation — first as a wounded dog whose maggots Asaṅga, moved by compassion, tried to remove with his tongue — and took him to Tuṣita, where he taught him the five treatises.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The name under which the five 'Dharmas of Maitreya' (Tibetan list) and, in Chinese tradition, the Yogācārabhūmi are transmitted; for the tradition, the future buddha Maitreya teaching Asaṅga.
notes: Whether a historical human teacher named Maitreya(nātha) existed is a scholarly question (Ui Hakuju argued yes; others treat the name as a pious attribution). The registry id is used for the author; the bodhisattva is tch:maitreya-bodhisattva (U39).

name: Asaṅga

tradition.text: lived 150 years (Tibetan histories); prophesied in the Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa

scholarly.text: c. 4th c. CE (often c. 310–390 or c. 330–405)

realization_account.text: Born in Puruṣapura as eldest of three brothers of a brahmin (Kauśika) family, he first ordained in the Mahīśāsaka (Paramārtha's account); dissatisfied with his understanding of emptiness, he meditated for twelve years in a cave, leaving three times in despair and each time turning back at a sign of perseverance; when compassion for a maggot-ridden dog finally opened his vision, Maitreya appeared and taught him in Tuṣita. He then converted his brother Vasubandhu.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder, with his half-brother Vasubandhu, of the Yogācāra school: author of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha and Abhidharmasamuccaya and, for the Tibetans, compiler of the Yogācārabhūmi and receiver of the Maitreya texts; in Tibetan tradition the founder of the 'lineage of vast conduct'.

name: Vasubandhu

scholarly.text: c. 4th–5th c. CE; E. Frauwallner proposed two Vasubandhus (an elder Yogācāra, a younger Kośa author) — a thesis now mostly abandoned but still cited

realization_account.text: A master of Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika who wrote the Abhidharmakośa and scorned the Mahāyāna, he was brought to it when Asaṅga, feigning illness, had him hear the Akṣayamatinirdeśa and Daśabhūmika; repenting, he wished to cut out his tongue, but Asaṅga told him to use that tongue to teach the Mahāyāna instead.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu, T2049; Tibetan histories)

summary: Author of the Abhidharmakośa and, after his conversion by Asaṅga, of the Twenty and Thirty Verses, the Three Natures and commentaries on the Maitreya texts; honoured in East Asia as the second patriarch of Yogācāra and in Tibet as one of the 'six ornaments'.
notes: U38 owns the Abhidharma side of this entry; U41 contributes the Yogācāra works and account.

name: Sthiramati

realization_account.text: Tāranātha tells that in a former life he was a pigeon who heard Vasubandhu recite the abhidharma daily, and was reborn human as a result.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great commentator of Valabhī whose Sanskrit commentaries on the Thirty Verses and the Madhyāntavibhāga are the classic Indian explanations of Yogācāra; in East Asian doxography the representative of the view that the seen and seeing parts of cognition are imagined, only the self-witnessing part real.

name: Dharmapāla (Yogācāra)

scholarly.text: c. 530–561 CE (Xuanzang's report that he died young; dates debated)

summary: Nālandā master whose interpretation of the Thirty Verses — four divisions of cognition, both innate and newly perfumed seeds — Xuanzang adopted as orthodox in the Cheng weishi lun; teacher of Śīlabhadra.
notes: Not the same as the Pāli commentator Dhammapāla (tch:dhammapala) or the Bengal king Dharmapāla.

name: Dignāga
places: Siṃhavakta near Kāñcī (birthplace in Tibetan accounts)

realization_account.text: Tibetan histories tell that he defeated the tīrthika Sudurjaya at Nālandā, and that while he was composing the Pramāṇasamuccaya in a cave, an opponent twice erased the opening verse he had written on the rock; when he considered abandoning the work for his own liberation, Mañjuśrī appeared and told him to compose it, promising to be his spiritual friend until awakening.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Bu ston; Tāranātha)

summary: Founder of the Buddhist pramāṇa school, pupil of Vasubandhu by tradition: the Pramāṇasamuccaya's two means of knowledge, perception free of construction, reflexive awareness, the triple mark of the reason and the exclusion theory of meaning; in Tibet one of the 'six ornaments'.

name: Īśvarasena
summary: Logician between Dignāga and Dharmakīrti — by Tibetan tradition Dignāga's pupil and Dharmakīrti's teacher — whose views (e.g. on non-perception as a separate means) Dharmakīrti criticized; no works survive.
notes: 'Pupil of Dignāga' is chronologically loose; recorded as the tradition's account.

name: Dharmakīrti

scholarly.text: c. 600–660 CE (older view c. 530–600; E. Frauwallner 600–660; H. Krasser argued for c. 550–610)

places: Trimalaya / Cūḍāmaṇi in the south (birthplace in Tibetan accounts)

realization_account.text: Born to a brahmin family in the south, he mastered the Vedas and, disillusioned, took up Buddhism; to learn his opponents' doctrine he served in disguise in the household of the Mīmāṃsaka Kumārila; he heard the Pramāṇasamuccaya from Īśvarasena, understood it better than his teacher, and with his permission composed the Pramāṇavārttika, defeating many opponents in debate; he died in Kaliṅga.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account (Bu ston; Tāranātha)

summary: The most influential Buddhist epistemologist, author of 'seven treatises on valid cognition': he grounded inference in necessary connection by identity or causality, recast exclusion, proved momentariness from causal efficacy, argued for rebirth and for the Buddha as a person of valid cognition, and refuted God and the authorless Veda; one of the Tibetan 'six ornaments'.
notes: The Kumārila service story is chronologically doubtful and is the tradition's.

name: Devendrabuddhi
summary: Dharmakīrti's disciple and first commentator on the Pramāṇavārttika; Tibetan tradition says Dharmakīrti rejected his first two drafts and accepted the third, saying that the literal sense was grasped but not the intent.

name: Śākyabuddhi
summary: Devendrabuddhi's pupil and author of a sub-commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika; Tibetan scholastics group him with Devendrabuddhi as commentators who follow the words closely (classification recalled).

name: Dharmottara
summary: Kashmiri(?) logician whose commentaries on the Nyāyabindu and Pramāṇaviniścaya shaped later Indian and early Tibetan epistemology; he stressed that a means of knowledge makes one attain (prāpaka) its object.

name: Prajñākaragupta
summary: Author of the Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra, a reading of Dharmakīrti that stresses the Buddha's authority, the ultimate non-duality of cognition and the path; Tibetan scholastics treat him as the head of a distinct line of commentators (classification recalled).

name: Jinendrabuddhi
summary: Commentator on Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, whose Viśālāmalavatī preserves much of Dignāga's Sanskrit.

name: Vinītadeva
summary: Nālandā commentator on Dharmakīrti's shorter treatises and on Vasubandhu's Twenty and Thirty Verses.

name: Arcaṭa
summary: Commentator on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu.

name: Durvekamiśra
summary: Bengali commentator on Dharmottara and Arcaṭa.

name: Karṇakagomin
summary: Commentator on Dharmakīrti's autocommentary to the Pramāṇavārttika.

name: Manorathanandin
summary: Author of the only complete Sanskrit commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika.

name: Jñānaśrīmitra
summary: Vikramaśīla scholar (by tradition one of its 'gate-keepers') whose works on momentariness, exclusion, God and the reality of cognition's images mark the height of late Indian Buddhist philosophy.

name: Ratnakīrti
summary: Jñānaśrīmitra's pupil at Vikramaśīla, author of concise proofs of momentariness and exclusion and refutations of God and of other mind-streams.

name: Ratnākaraśānti
summary: Vikramaśīla scholar (by tradition 'gate-keeper' of the eastern gate) and tantric master, counted among the eighty-four mahāsiddhas as Śāntipa; the chief defender of image-less (nirākāra / alīkākāra) Yogācāra and teacher of Atiśa.

name: Jitāri
summary: Logician of Bengal, by tradition a teacher of Atiśa, author of short manuals of logic and of works on exclusion and universals.

name: Mokṣākaragupta
summary: Logician of the Jagaddala monastery, author of the Tarkabhāṣā.

name: Śaṅkarasvāmin
summary: Pupil of Dignāga (Chinese tradition) and author of the Nyāyapraveśa, the primer of East Asian logic.

name: Śaṅkaranandana
summary: Kashmiri Buddhist logician, known as 'the brahmin', author of works on exclusion and necessary connection and of a commentary on the Pramāṇavārttika.

name: Śubhagupta
alt_names: Kalyāṇarakṣita (back-translation of the Tibetan dge srung)
summary: Buddhist logician who, unusually, defended external objects against Yogācāra, while otherwise following Dharmakīrti (omniscience, exclusion, refutation of God and the Veda).

name: Asvabhāva
summary: Yogācāra commentator on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha and the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra.

name: Guṇamati
summary: Yogācāra master of Valabhī reported by Xuanzang, teacher of Sthiramati and one of the ten masters of the Cheng weishi lun.

name: Śīlabhadra
summary: Abbot of Nālandā, pupil of Dharmapāla, who taught Xuanzang the Yogācārabhūmi; Xuanzang reports that he was cured of a painful illness after being told in a dream to await a Chinese monk.

name: Kuiji
summary: Xuanzang's principal disciple and systematizer of Faxiang, counted its first patriarch; author of the great commentaries on the Cheng weishi lun and the Nyāyapraveśa and champion of the five-gotra doctrine.

name: Wŏnch'ŭk
summary: Silla Korean monk in Chang'an who studied with Xuanzang but, integrating Paramārtha's teachings, differed from Kuiji; his Saṃdhinirmocana commentary was translated into Tibetan.

name: Huiguang
summary: Chinese Vinaya and Dilun master, founder of the southern branch of the Dilun school.

name: Dōshō
summary: Japanese monk who studied with Xuanzang and brought Hossō (Yogācāra) teaching to Japan.

name: Candragomin
summary: Lay Yogācāra master and grammarian (Cāndra-vyākaraṇa); Tibetan tradition tells of his long debate with Candrakīrti at Nālandā, Yogācāra against Madhyamaka, and of his devotion to Tārā and Avalokiteśvara.

name: Haribhadra (Buddhist)
summary: Yogācāra-Madhyamaka commentator on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra under King Dharmapāla of Bengal; not the Jain Haribhadra (tch:haribhadra).

name: Ārya Vimuktisena
summary: Earliest known commentator on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.

name: Jinaputra
summary: Yogācāra commentator, one of the ten masters of the Cheng weishi lun; credited in Tibet with the Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya.

name: Sumatiśīla
summary: Commentator on Vasubandhu's Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa (Tibetan).

name: Nanda (Yogācāra master)
summary: One of the ten Indian masters of the Cheng weishi lun, reported as holding that all seeds are newly perfumed and that cognition has only two parts (seeing and seen).

name: Sajjana
summary: Kashmiri paṇḍita who taught the Maitreya texts to Ngok Loden Sherab and Tsen Kawoche, source of the Tibetan 'analytic' and 'meditative' transmissions of the Maitreya teachings.

name: Chapa Chökyi Senge
alt_names: phya pa chos kyi seng ge
summary: Abbot of Sangphu and leading early Tibetan epistemologist, credited with the Collected Topics debate method.

name: Khedrup Je Gelek Pelzang
alt_names: mkhas grub dge legs dpal bzang
summary: Tsongkhapa's disciple and author of the Gelug epistemological summa Tshad ma sde bdun gyi rgyan yid kyi mun sel.

name: Paramārtha
summary: Indian translator in southern China whose versions of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha and related works founded the Shelun school; he taught a ninth, 'stainless' consciousness (amalavijñāna) identical with suchness, and wrote the Life of Vasubandhu.
notes: Contribution of U41; U39 and U54 also emit this id.

name: Xuanzang
summary: Chinese pilgrim-translator who studied the Yogācārabhūmi at Nālandā under Śīlabhadra, won a celebrated debate at Kanyākubja under King Harṣa, and on his return translated the Yogācāra corpus and compiled the Cheng weishi lun, founding Faxiang.

name: Śāntarakṣita
summary: Nālandā abbot and founder of Yogācāra-Madhyamaka, who also wrote the Tattvasaṃgraha — the great Dharmakīrtian critique of rival systems — and a commentary on the Vādanyāya.

name: Kamalaśīla
summary: Śāntarakṣita's disciple, commentator on the Tattvasaṃgraha and author of the Bhāvanākramas, which quote the Laṅkāvatāra's four-stage entry through mind-only.
notes: Contribution of U41 (pramāṇa and Yogācāra side).

name: Sakya Paṇḍita Kunga Gyaltsen
summary: Sakya hierarch whose Treasury of Reasoning re-established Dharmakīrti's denial of real universals in Tibetan epistemology.
notes: Contribution of U41 (pramāṇa side); U47 owns.

name: Gyaltsab Je Darma Rinchen
summary: Tsongkhapa's disciple, author of the standard Gelug commentaries on the Pramāṇavārttika and the Abhisamayālaṃkāra.

name: Ngok Loden Sherab
summary: Translator of the Pramāṇaviniścaya, Pramāṇavārttikālaṅkāra and the Maitreya texts, founder of the Sangphu scholastic tradition of epistemology and Madhyamaka.

name: Maitrīpa

realization_account.text: Tibetan tradition holds that Maitrīpa rediscovered the Dharmadharmatāvibhāga and the Ratnagotravibhāga, hidden in a stūpa, after a vision of Maitreya.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Indian mahāsiddha and scholar (c. 1007–1085) credited in Tibet with recovering two Maitreya texts.
notes: Contribution of U41; U44/U46 own the entry.

name: Tsongkhapa Lobsang Drakpa
summary: Founder of the Gelug school; his Essence of Eloquence and treatise on mind and the store-consciousness are the Tibetan reference expositions of Cittamātra.
